accepted.s: Which one of the following Acts specifically penalises brothels, pimping and living off the earnings of prostitution?
o: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
accepted.x: The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 penalises brothels, pimping and living off another person’s earnings from prostitution.
accepted.tq: Use the scope of the statute to distinguish it from neighbouring labour and child-protection laws.
accepted.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

accepted.s: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 is primarily concerned with the abolition of
accepted.x: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 abolishes bonded labour, including debt bondage found in sectors such as brick kilns, agriculture and domestic work.
accepted.tq: Match the statute with its precise subject rather than with a related constitutional article.
accepted.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act — 1956
2. Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act — 1976
3. Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act — 1986
4. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — 2023
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
accepted.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The respective years are 1956, 1976, 1986 and 2023.
accepted.tq: Verify each year independently before selecting the coded combination.
accepted.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

accepted.s: The 2016 amendment to the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act provided that
o: no person below eighteen years may work in any occupation
children below twelve years may work in non-hazardous factories
only bonded labour by children was prohibited
no child below fourteen years may work in any occupation, while adolescents aged fourteen to eighteen may not work in hazardous occupations
accepted.x: The 2016 amendment prohibited employment of children below fourteen years in any occupation and prohibited adolescents aged fourteen to eighteen from hazardous work.
accepted.tq: Separate the two age bands and their different prohibitions.
accepted.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

accepted.s:
With reference to trafficking under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, consider the following statements:
1. Trafficking is dealt with under Section 143.
2. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024.
3. The consent of a victim is immaterial for determining the trafficking offence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct: Section 143 addresses trafficking, the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024, and victim consent does not validate trafficking.
accepted.tq: Check the section number, commencement date and legal effect of consent as separate details.
accepted.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

accepted.s: Which of the following is associated with the institutional response to human trafficking?
o: District Anti-Human Trafficking Units funded by the Ministry of Home Affairs
State Finance Commissions funded by the Election Commission
District Legal Services Authorities funded by the Reserve Bank of India
National Human Rights Courts funded by the Ministry of Education
accepted.x: District Anti-Human Trafficking Units are associated with the response to trafficking and are funded by the Ministry of Home Affairs. The POCSO Act, 2012 is also a linked child-protection law.
accepted.tq: Identify the correct ministry-body association and reject swapped institutional authorities.
accepted.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

accepted.s: Which one of the following rights is available to every religious denomination or any section thereof, subject to public order, morality and health?
o: The right to exempt all property from regulation by law
The right to compel religious instruction in every school
The right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion
The right to impose a tax for religious purposes
accepted.x: Article 26 gives every religious denomination or section thereof the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, subject to public order, morality and health.
accepted.tq: Ask who holds the right and then apply the constitutional limitations.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 26:
1. A religious denomination may establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes.
2. It may own and acquire movable and immovable property.
3. It may administer its property in accordance with law.
4. These rights are subject to public order, morality and health.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Article 26 includes all four rights and expressly subjects them to public order, morality and health.
accepted.tq: Test the complete set of clauses and the common constitutional limitations together.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s: Article 27 prohibits
o: every fee imposed by a public authority in connection with a religious institution
compelling a person to pay taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically used to promote a particular religion
all public expenditure benefiting religious communities equally
the State from regulating secular administration of religious institutions
accepted.x: Article 27 bars compulsory payment of taxes whose proceeds are used to promote a particular religion. It does not bar all fees or expenditure benefiting all religions equally.
accepted.tq: Distinguish a tax from a fee and a particular-religion purpose from equal public support.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 27 is correct?
o: Taxes may be collected only for the promotion of the majority religion.
A fee for the secular administration of a religious institution is permissible.
Article 27 applies only to religious denominations and not to individuals.
Every fee connected with a religious institution is unconstitutional.
accepted.x: Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a particular religion, but a fee imposed for secular administration of a religious institution is permissible.
accepted.tq: Find the precise exception instead of treating the constitutional prohibition as absolute.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
(a) Article 26
(b) Article 27
(c) Article 28(1)
(d) Article 28(3)

List-II (Subject)
(i) No person compelled to attend religious instruction without consent
(ii) Religious denomination’s right to manage religious affairs
(iii) No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
(iv) No compulsory tax for promotion of a particular religion

Select the correct answer using the code below.
accepted.x: Article 26 concerns denominational religious affairs; Article 27 concerns taxes; Article 28(1) concerns State-funded religious instruction; and Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure Article 27 pair and then complete the Article 28 distinctions.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s: A State-administered educational institution was established under a trust or endowment that requires religious instruction. Under Article 28, such instruction is
o: permitted because the institution is administered by the State and the trust requires it
permitted only if every student belongs to the same religion
permitted only in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
accepted.x: Article 28(2) does not apply the prohibition to a State-administered institution established under an endowment or trust requiring religious instruction.
accepted.tq: Apply the trust/endowment exception rather than relying only on the institution’s State administration.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s: In a State-recognised or State-aided educational institution, attendance at religious instruction
o: is prohibited even when the student and guardian consent
may be compelled by the head of the institution
cannot be compelled without the individual’s consent; in the case of a minor, the guardian’s consent is required
is compulsory if the institution receives State aid
accepted.x: Article 28(3) prevents compulsion to attend religious instruction in State-recognised or aided institutions. For a minor, the guardian’s consent is required.
accepted.tq: Track the difference between prohibition of instruction and prohibition of compulsory attendance.
accepted.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

accepted.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam
B. Orissa Freedom of Religion Act
C. Stanislaus decision upholding such laws
D. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita coming into force in place of the IPC
accepted.x: The Orissa Act was enacted in 1967, the Madhya Pradesh law in 1968, Stanislaus was decided in 1977, and the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.
accepted.tq: Fix the two adjacent enactment years first, then place the judgment and the BNS.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967 and the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968 were initially enacted primarily in response to concerns about
o: sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib
accepted.x: Both early State laws arose from concerns over missionary activity. Later amendments widened their scope to conversions to Islam as well.
accepted.tq: Identify the original policy concern and distinguish it from later amendments.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: Which one of the following best describes the significance of the Stanislaus v. Madhya Pradesh decision, 1977?
o: It prohibited every form of religious propagation.
It declared all State conversion laws unconstitutional.
It held that propagation necessarily includes a right to convert another person by force.
It upheld State conversion laws and held that propagation does not include forcible conversion.
accepted.x: In Stanislaus v. Madhya Pradesh, 1977, such State laws were upheld and propagation was held not to include forcible conversion.
accepted.tq: Separate propagation from forcible conversion, the central conceptual distinction in the case.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: The later amendments to certain State freedom-of-religion laws widened their scope from concerns over Christian missionary activity to include conversions to
accepted.x: The later amendments widened the scope of the laws to cover conversions to Islam in addition to the earlier concern over Christian missionary activity.
accepted.tq: Test the specific expansion of scope rather than the general existence of conversion laws.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code, concerning deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings, was upheld in
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accepted.x: Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh upheld Section 295A on public-order grounds. The corresponding provision is now Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
accepted.tq: Match the case with the statutory provision and its constitutional ground.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Section 295A of the IPC is now reflected as Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
2. The provision concerns deliberate outrage of religious feelings.
3. It was upheld in Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh on public-order grounds.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Section 299 of the BNS corresponds to the earlier Section 295A, which was upheld in Ramji Lal Modi on public-order grounds.
accepted.tq: Combine the old provision, new provision and leading case instead of confusing the two section numbers.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: The Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, which received assent in April 2026, is associated with
o: compulsory religious instruction in Punjab schools
removal of Article 27 restrictions on religious taxes
abolition of all State conversion laws in Punjab
a maximum punishment of life imprisonment for sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib
accepted.x: The Punjab amendment allows punishment of up to life imprisonment for sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib. It has been challenged before the Punjab and Haryana High Court on the ground that it protects only one faith.
accepted.tq: Use the distinctive statute name and punishment while avoiding confusion with general conversion legislation.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: A challenge to the Punjab sacrilege legislation referred to above has been made before the
o: Supreme Court of India exclusively on taxation grounds
Delhi High Court on the ground that it abolishes religious freedom
Punjab and Haryana High Court on the ground that it protects only one faith
Madhya Pradesh High Court on the ground that it permits forcible conversion
accepted.x: The Act has been challenged in the Punjab and Haryana High Court on the ground that it protects only one faith.
accepted.tq: Identify the forum and the precise constitutional objection rather than a related religious-freedom issue.
accepted.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the scope of Article 24?
o: It applies only to children employed by the State.
It prohibits only bonded labour by children below fourteen years.
It prohibits employment below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment, but does not bar harmless or innocent work.
It prohibits every kind of work by every person below eighteen years.
accepted.x: Article 24 is directed at employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment; harmless or innocent work is not covered by the constitutional prohibition.
accepted.tq: Reject the overbroad ‘every kind of work’ statement and retain the hazardous-employment limit.
accepted.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

accepted.s: The 2016 amendment renamed the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as the
o: Protection of Children from Hazardous Work Act
Child Rights and Bonded Labour Act
accepted.x: The 2016 amendment renamed the statute as the Child and Adolescent Labour Act and introduced the present age-based restrictions.
accepted.tq: Test the exact statutory title, a common look-alike wording trap.
accepted.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

accepted.s:
Under the amended child-labour framework, which statement is correct?
1. A child below fourteen years is generally barred from work, subject to the stated exception for family enterprise after school hours.
2. An adolescent aged fourteen to eighteen years is barred from hazardous work.
3. The Right to Education Act, 2009 covers the age group of six to fourteen years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The amended law has the family-enterprise-after-school exception for children, prohibits hazardous work by adolescents, and the RTE Act covers children aged six to fourteen years.
accepted.tq: Keep the three age ranges and exceptions separate before choosing the combination.
accepted.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

accepted.s: The Right to Education Act, 2009 gives effect to which constitutional provision for children aged six to fourteen years?
accepted.x: The Right to Education Act, 2009 gives effect to Article 21A, which concerns free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the education guarantee from the child-labour prohibition and DPSP provisions.
accepted.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

accepted.s: The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 provides the statutory basis for the
o: National Human Rights Commission and State Human Rights Commissions
National Commission for Minorities and District Anti-Human Trafficking Units
National Commission for Women and State Finance Commissions
National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights
accepted.x: The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 provides for the NCPCR and SCPCRs.
accepted.tq: Match the Act with the bodies it creates and avoid swapping similarly named commissions.
accepted.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

accepted.s:
Which of the following Directive Principles is directly related to protection of children from abuse and exploitation?
1. Article 39(e)
2. Article 39(f)
3. Article 44
4. Article 48A
Select the correct answer using the code below.
accepted.x: Articles 39(e) and 39(f) direct the State to ensure that the tender age of children is not abused and that children develop in a healthy manner with protection against exploitation.
accepted.tq: Use the subject matter of the Directive Principle to eliminate unrelated provisions.
accepted.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws
